doc.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Rock, Tonight Show and early career
title: Big band versus combo drumming and the changing work scene
summary: Tonight Show drummers needed both rock and jazz; big band drumming needs a fuller sound than combo playing, and non-adapters lost work as jazz clubs closed.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Of course. Well if he had a jazz guest on the show and you had a person in the drum chair who could just do Rock stuff, they would say the same complaint.

They would say the same thing. Yeah, that’s a very good point. That’s right. I couldn’t call a guy who was a straight Rock player either, because his jazz stuff would be too weak. And big band jazz I think you really have to have a little more experience at than © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-

small band jazz. What I mean is you have to have had also some big band jazz experience, not just combo experience. Because most combo drummers don’t speak with a big enough sound for a big band. They don’t know how to get a bigger sound. It’s not a case of louder, it’s a case of fuller. Like a good lead alto player, what does he need? A good, full sound, right? It’s sort of like that. Or a good lead trumpet player. You have to know how to generate a fuller sound for that. So anyway, our original question, I hope we didn’t wander off it, was that yes, some players adapted, and I’d say some players did not. And the players that did not soon found the work was really trickling away from them because there was such a little bit of jazz going on, even around New York. I mean the jazz clubs were all closing up, and it was a kind of a different scene that was going on.
